FXI is activated directly by α-thrombins lacking an intact ABE-I, and indirectly by FXIIa.
thrombin forms other than α-throbmin contribute directly to feedback FXI activation in plasma and FXIa provides a link between TF-initiated coagulaiton and contact system proteases.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanism of thrombin generation, the role of thrombin in the coagulation process, and the role of thrombomodulin in the regulation of thrombin activity and fibrin formation.
the mechanism of action of the coagulation proteases and their role in the initiation of blood coagulation.
the mechanism of activation of the zymogen FXI to the serine protease FXIa, a key enzyme in coagulation and fibrinolysis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
thrombin is the main activator of FXI.
FXI activation can be initiated by α-thrombins, β-thrombins, and γ-thrombins, with α-thrombins being the least efficient.
thrombin activation of factor XI in the prothrombin complex is a critical step for amplification of the coagulation cascade.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the prothrombinse complex can activate factor XI through two different mechanisms: 1) through the direct activation by α-thromin, and 2) through the indirect activation by FXIa, formed by the FXIIa-mediated activation of FXI.
FXI is activated through the action of multiple thrombin forms and FXIa can contribute to thrombin formation through activation of FXII.
the FXIa/FXI feedback loop is a major source of α-thrombin during coagulation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the prothrombin fragment 1 (F1), which is a fragment of prothrombom that is generated when prothrombin is converted to thrombin, is a potent activator of factor XI.
FXI activation is not limited to α-thrombins and that other forms of thrombin, such as β- and γ-thrombins and thrombins with ABE I mutations, can activate FXI in plasma.
thrombin can activate factor XI in a variety of ways and that factor XI activation by thrombin may be more important in vivo than previously thought.
